docs.text: Parameter Default Description width 64 Horizontal resolution (pixels) height 48 Image rows (1 = single strip) fov 90° Horizontal field of view center_angle 0° Center offset from robot heading vertical_angle 0° Camera tilt — positive = tilted down (ground), negative = tilted up (sky). At 90° the camera looks straight down at the floor. max_range 10.0 Not used by the MuJoCo render (kept for saved networks) fps 60 Frames per simulated second (0 = as fast as possible) lateralized False Split output into left/right halves overlap 0 Pixels past midline included in each half

docs.title: SkyCompassSensor
docs.text:
Encodes the robot's heading relative to the sun via a cosine tuning curve, mimicking insect dorsal rim area (DRA) photoreceptors.

Always senses, whether or not the polarization field is shown in the arena — the "Sky: Polarization field" checkbox and drag control only set/display the sun direction, they don't gate sensing.

docs.title: Tuning curve
docs.text:
Per neuron k:

\[r_k = \cos\!\left(\theta - \phi_{\text{sun}} - \phi_0 - k \cdot \frac{2\pi}{n}\right) \times \text{scale}\]

where \(\phi_{\text{sun}} = \text{sky.angle} + \pi/2\) (perpendicular to e-vector bars) and \(\phi_0\) = phase.

docs.title: Output pipeline
docs.text: \[\tau = \begin{cases}\tau_{rise} & r > x \\ \tau_{decay} & r \leq x\end{cases}, \quad \frac{dx}{dt} = \frac{r - x}{\tau}\] \[\text{output} = f(x) \quad (\text{or}\ f(r)\ \text{if no dynamics})\]

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Description n Number of DRA neurons (heading directions sampled) phase Rotates neuron 0 to align with a reference direction output_mode none / derivative (heading change detection) / integral noise_std / noise_tau Additive Ornstein–Uhlenbeck noise on raw signal

docs.title: Neuromodulation
docs.text: Receptors (modulators) and the transmitter act on the sensor's neuron stage (the Neuron tab of its dialog), not on the reading itself.

docs.title: WhiskerSensor
docs.text: Casts a ray from a mount point along the body heading. Output is bending proportion: 0 = no contact, 1 = contact at the base.

docs.title: Mount pose
docs.text:
\[\text{origin} = \bigl(x + d_m\cos(\theta + \alpha_m),\; y + d_m\sin(\theta + \alpha_m)\bigr)\]

where \(d_m\) = mount_dist, \(\alpha_m\) = mount_angle.

docs.title: Raw signal
docs.text:
\[r = \text{clip}\!\left(\frac{\text{length} - d}{\text{length}},\; 0,\; 1\right) \times \text{scale}\]

where \(d\) = distance to first obstacle. If no contact: \(r = 0\).

docs.title: Output pipeline
docs.text: \[\tau = \begin{cases}\tau_{rise} & r > x \\ \tau_{decay} & r \leq x\end{cases}, \quad \frac{dx}{dt} = \frac{r - x}{\tau}\] \[\text{output} = f(x) \quad (\text{or}\ f(r)\ \text{if no dynamics})\]

docs.title: Surviving in Buridan's World
docs.text:
Buridan's ass is a centuries-old thought experiment: a donkey stands exactly midway between two identical, equally appetizing bales of hay. With no reason to prefer either one, it can never decide — and starves to death standing still.

This tutorial picks up from Braitenberg Vehicle III and puts its "love" circuit in exactly that bind: two gradient patches, placed as mirror images of each other, with one patch ever so slightly stronger than the other. You'll see the direct wiring from Vehicle III fail to resolve even a large difference, then build two more vehicles — Waverer and Rivalry — each using the same sensory machinery more cleverly to push the resolution limit further.

What you will build

Step What happens Add a second, mirrored patch Two A patches, equidistant from the robot Confirm the tie With both patches identical, the robot drives straight between them forever Set a quantity difference One patch at 1.0, the other swept from 0.9 down — find where Vehicle III fails Widen the steering wiring Builds Waverer: a pure left-vs-right comparator Run Waverer Find the quantity difference it can no longer resolve Insert a competing pair Builds Rivalry: mutual inhibition that commits to one side Run Rivalry Find its resolution limit — smaller than Waverer's

docs.title: Background — a tie needs something to break it
docs.text:
Every circuit you've built so far is purely feedforward: a sensor reading flows straight to a motor command, deterministically. Put two identical stimuli in front of the robot, symmetric left and right, and the circuit has nowhere to go — equal inputs produce equal outputs, forever.

Breaking a tie needs two things: an amplifier that turns a small difference into a growing one, and a seed to start from. The amplifier is mutual inhibition — two neurons that suppress each other. The seed, in this tutorial, is a real difference in the world: one patch is fractionally stronger than the other. The question is how small that difference can be and still reliably steer the robot.

docs.title: Step 1 — Reopen your Vehicle III network
docs.text:
Launch the simulator and reopen the network you built in Vehicle III, with light (a GradientSensor, n=2, gradient='A') wired for approach — cruise (a ConstantLayer, value 60) feeding motor directly, and light inhibiting motor same-side (Vehicle III, Step 5).

Keep light's noise_std = 0 throughout this tutorial — you want the only asymmetry to come from the world, not from sensor noise.

Skipped Vehicle III?

Build that starting point first: a GradientSensor named light (n=2, gradient='A', scale=60), a ConstantLayer named cruise (n=2, value=60) wired to motor with the identity matrix, and light → motor wired same-side with weight −1 on the diagonal. See Braitenberg Vehicle III for the full build.

docs.title: Step 2 — Give it two identical choices
docs.text:
1. Go to the World tab. If you don't already have an A patch placed ahead of the robot, place one now (as in Vehicle II/III).
  2. Hold Ctrl and drag the patch — this clones it, the same size and colour, following your cursor while the original stays put.
  3. Hold Shift at the same time to snap both the original and the clone to the grid. Drop the clone so it mirrors the original across the robot's forward axis — same distance, opposite side.

Give it room

If the arena feels cramped with two patches in it, increase arena_scale in the Physics tab so the robot has more distance to react before it reaches either one.

docs.title: Step 3 — Confirm the tie
docs.text: Press ▶ Run. With both patches at their default quantity (1.0) and no sensor noise, the two eyes always read exactly the same value. The robot drives straight between the patches and never turns. This is Buridan's ass at its most literal: perfectly symmetric, perfectly stuck.

docs.title: Step 4 — Set a quantity difference
docs.text:
Double-click one of the patches and leave its quantity at 1.0. Double-click the other and set its quantity to 0.9 — it now peaks at 0.9 instead of 1.0 at its centre, while looking identical on screen.

What patch quantity does

Quantity is a multiplier on the patch's signal before the sensor reads it. A patch with quantity q produces a reading of q × r where r is the raw distance-based gradient value in [0, 1]. The two patches are otherwise identical in size, position, and label — only the quantity differs.

Press ▶ Run. The robot should now reliably turn toward the stronger patch. Then tighten the difference: set the second patch to 0.99, run again. Then 0.999, then 0.9999. At some point Vehicle III stops committing reliably before reaching either patch — record that threshold. This is the resolution limit of plain same-side inhibition.

docs.title: Step 5 — Widen the steering wiring: Waverer
docs.text:
One of evolution's recurring solutions to telling two similar stimuli apart is to rewire the same inputs so that small differences are amplified rather than passed through unchanged. In Vehicle III each motor neuron listens to only one eye; adding a crossed excitatory term means each motor neuron now receives excitation from one eye and inhibition from the other — the motor layer becomes the comparator, and what drives it is no longer each eye's absolute reading but the difference between them.

  1. In the network visualizer, right-click the light → motor connection and choose Edit weight….

  2. Switch to Manual and enter:

    light_0 (left) light_1 (right) motor_0 (left wheel) −1 +1 motor_1 (right wheel) +1 −1

  3. Confirm and Save.

Call this vehicle Waverer — a robot that wavers between two choices, pulled equally by both. It already embodies a key evolutionary strategy: suppress the common signal, amplify the difference. But it has no memory and no way to sharpen a difference that is too small to act on.

Writing Δ = light_0 − light_1, the matrix gives left = 60 − Δ, right = 60 + Δ. Total speed stays fixed at 120; only its split between the wheels changes.

Press ▶ Run starting from the quantity difference that defeated Vehicle III. Keep tightening the difference — 0.99, 0.999, 0.9999 — until Waverer also fails. That is Waverer's resolution floor, and exactly the problem the next steps address.

docs.title: Step 6 — Insert a competing pair: Rivalry
docs.text:
In Waverer there is no decision as such — the motor neurons receive sensory input and move. The "choice" is the motor output itself, happening at the last possible moment, with no internal deliberation before it. One of evolution's key innovations was to push that process upstream: to create circuits inside the brain that compete, settle on an outcome, and only then instruct the motor system what to do. The sensor readings go in; a committed signal comes out; the muscles just follow.

  1. Delete the existing light → motor connection from Step 5.
  2. Drag an AdaptiveLayer chip onto the canvas, between light and motor. Name it choice, set n = 2.

  3. In choice's settings set:

    • tau_rise → 0.1, tau_decay → 0.1
    • w → 1.0 — the cross-inhibition weight: each neuron subtracts the other's output from its own input.
    • beta → 0.0 — AdaptiveLayer defaults this to 1.0, which turns on fatigue: a neuron that fires strongly for too long gradually suppresses itself, producing burst-and-fade behaviour. That is biologically important — it prevents any single neuron from monopolising the circuit indefinitely — but here you want the winner to hold its lead, not tire out. Set beta to 0 so choice only competes, with no fatigue on top.

    Fatigue and oscillators

    When both w and beta are nonzero, the same mutual-inhibition circuit stops locking and starts alternating — each side wins, fatigues, loses, recovers, and wins again. That rhythm is the basis of a central pattern generator, the kind of circuit that drives walking, swimming, and breathing in real animals. It is a topic for another session; see AdaptiveLayer if you want to explore it now.

  4. Wire light → choice, same-side only:

    light_0 (left) light_1 (right) choice_0 +1 0 choice_1 0 +1

  5. Wire choice → motor, same-side inhibitory:

    choice_0 choice_1 motor_0 (left wheel) −1 0 motor_1 (right wheel) 0 −1

  6. Save.

choice_0 is excited by the left eye and inhibited by choice_1's output; choice_1 is the mirror image. Whichever one edges ahead suppresses the other a little more than it's suppressed back, letting it edge further ahead: a positive feedback loop. Because choice's activation is relu, the losing neuron is floored at zero and can't recover — the decision sticks.

This is Rivalry: recurrent mutual inhibition, winner-take-all.

docs.title: Step 7 — Run Rivalry: find its resolution limit
docs.text:
Press ▶ Run starting from the quantity difference that defeated Waverer. Rivalry should commit to the stronger patch. Keep tightening — 0.999, 0.9999, 0.99999 — until Rivalry also fails to commit reliably.

Open the oscilloscope on choice_0 and choice_1 while it runs: you'll see both rise together briefly, then diverge — one to its ceiling, the other clamped at zero. The stronger patch wins consistently because the quantity difference gives one competitor a persistent head start, not a random one.

Oscillations after the decision

Once Rivalry commits, the robot curves hard toward the chosen patch — but as it closes in, the winning eye's signal grows and the same-side inhibition on the motor overdraws, causing overshoot and oscillation. The decision is stable; the approach is not. To damp it, increase tau_rise and tau_decay on choice so the competition integrates over time rather than reacting to every fluctuation.

docs.title: Challenge 1 — Bump, back up, turn away
docs.text:
Build a vehicle that drives forward by default and, on collision, backs away and turns away from the side that made contact, then resumes. Use a CollisionSensor (see CollisionSensor) in place of light.

This circuit needs noise

With a CollisionSensor there are no gradient patches to create an asymmetry — both bumpers are equally likely to fire first in a head-on collision. Set light's noise_std to a small value (try 0.05) so tiny random differences between the two bumper readings are enough to tip the turn direction. noise_std on the CollisionSensor plays the same role the patch quantity difference played in the main tutorial: it seeds the asymmetry the circuit then amplifies.

Split forward and backward into separate pathways

Give motor two separate drives: a forward pathway fed only by cruise, and a backward pathway fed only by the collision sensor, wired same-side or crossed depending on which way you want it to turn while backing away.

The sensor goes quiet before the response should

A bumper is a digital signal — it reads 1 while contact is live and drops back to 0 the instant it breaks. By the time the robot has reversed even slightly, the sensor is already silent, long before the robot is actually clear. Insert a dynamics layer between the sensor and the backward pathway and set tau_decay much longer than tau_rise: the layer charges fast on contact and drains slowly after, holding the reverse command alive long enough to actually escape. As an extra challenge, think about how to introduce an asymmetry so that one wheel backs away more than the other when both bumpers fire at once — giving the robot a preferred turning direction even in a head-on collision.

docs.title: Challenge 2 — Take it to the real robot
docs.text:
Once Challenge 1 works in simulation, run the same network on physical hardware — see Running Networks on the Real Robot. Set robot_address on the sensor and on motor. A CollisionSensor with n=2 matches the real robot's two bumpers directly; no rewiring needed.

Bumper address

Set the CollisionSensor's robot_address to 192.168.0.224:2390/bumpers[iiiii](1,2) — indices 1 and 2 are the front-left and front-right bumpers (index 0 is the packet counter). See Running Networks on the Real Robot for the full packet layout.

docs.title: Challenge 3 — Amplify the difference further
docs.text:
New circuits need tuning — and so did evolution

Adding a new pathway on top of an existing one rarely works out of the box. The weights, time constants, and scales of the new circuit have to be balanced against those already there, or the old behaviour breaks. This is not a quirk of simulation — it is exactly the pressure evolution faced every time a new circuit was added to an existing brain. Natural selection had to find weight combinations that preserved what worked while allowing something new to emerge. Expect to spend time rebalancing; that tuning effort is part of what you are learning.

There are several ways to push the circuit's resolution limit even further. Try one or more of the following, and compare how each one shifts the smallest quantity difference the robot can still resolve:

  • Contralateral input to choice. The light → choice connection is same-side only — each eye feeds its own competitor. Add a crossed inhibitory term so each eye also suppresses the rival competitor before the competition even starts, sharpening the initial asymmetry.
  • Waverer and Rivalry in parallel. Nature rarely replaces one circuit with another — it layers new ones on top. Restore the direct light → motor comparator from Step 5 alongside the existing choice → motor pathway. The motor neurons now receive two independent votes: one fast and feedforward, one slow and recurrent.
  • Feed the decision back to the sensors. Wire choice back onto light — crossed and inhibitory — so the winning side suppresses the losing eye's own signal at its source. This is inhibition of lateral inhibition: the winner starves the loser of input rather than just out-competing it downstream. Tighten the quantity difference to find whether this lets the circuit resolve differences that defeat plain Rivalry.

Sensors can be connection targets too

Every sensor has a neuron stage after its raw reading that the network reads from. You can wire onto a sensor exactly like a layer — the connection sums into that stage. See Sensors — neuron stage. light's neuron stage is pass-through by default; no settings changes needed.

docs.text:
• Wiring Brains — more general-purpose layer types and wiring patterns, including other ways dynamics layers reshape a sensor's signal before it reaches the motors.
  • AdaptiveLayer — the full layer reference, including the half-centre oscillator mode (beta > 0 together with w > 0) this tutorial deliberately avoided.
  • Creating Worlds — all the patch, obstacle, and duplication/grid-snap tools used in Step 2.

docs.title: Braitenberg Vehicle II
docs.text:
This tutorial builds a complete, working robot behaviour from scratch — world, sensors, and motor wiring — entirely through the simulator's graphical network editor. You will be programming behavior with neurons — no code required.

You will discover how just two sensor neurons wired to two motor neurons can produce what looks like aggression or fear, and how swapping two connection weights is all it takes to switch from one to the other.

What you will build

Step What happens Place a gradient patch The arena has a single red stimulus cloud Wire attraction Crossed connections — the robot steers toward the patch Flip to avoidance Swap two weights — the robot now flees the same patch

docs.title: Background — Braitenberg's insight
docs.text:
In 1984, Valentino Braitenberg described a series of imaginary vehicles. Each had sensors on the front and motors on the sides. He showed that incredibly simple wiring rules produce surprisingly rich behaviour:

  • Crossed wiring (left sensor → right motor, right sensor → left motor): when the stimulus is stronger on the left, the right motor speeds up and the robot steers toward it — aggression.
  • Same-side wiring (left sensor → left motor, right sensor → right motor): when the stimulus is stronger on the left, the left motor speeds up and the robot steers away — cowardice.

That is the whole secret. No computation, no memory, no planning — just which wire goes where.

docs.title: Step 1 — Launch the simulator
docs.text:
Double-click the LBP Simulator shortcut on your Desktop, or LBPSimulator (start.bat; ./start.sh on macOS/Linux) in the app folder. See Installing if you haven't set it up yet.

The main window opens. You will see a Controls panel on the left with a Brain / World / Session / Physics / Robot / Network tab bar, and the arena — the large circular area on the right — with the robot disc sitting near the centre.

docs.title: Step 1b — Take it for a drive
docs.text:
Before adding any sensors or wiring, get a feel for how the robot moves.

Press ▶ Run to start the simulation. The robot won't move on its own yet — there is no brain loaded — but you can steer it manually with the keyboard:

Key Action W Both wheels forward S Both wheels backward A Spin left D Spin right

Drive it around the arena for a moment. Notice how the two independent wheels work: turning is just running one wheel faster than the other — the same principle the brain will use later.

Robot moving too fast?

Tick the Real Time checkbox in the Controls panel. This caps the simulation to real-world speed, which makes the robot much easier to drive.

Press ■ Stop when you're done. The world resets to its starting position for the next step.

docs.title: Step 2 — Place a gradient patch
docs.text:
A gradient patch is an invisible circular stimulus cloud; you can think of it as an abstraction of an environmental gradient like an odor, or termperature, or light. The robot's sensors detect its signal; the robot's body passes through it without pysical resistance.

  1. Click the World tab in the Controls panel.
  2. In the Gradients row, click the A button (the pinkish-red one — it creates a gradient with label A).
  3. Move your cursor onto the arena, somewhere in front of the robot — toward the upper half of the arena.
  4. Click and drag: the drag start becomes the patch centre; the drag end sets its radius. Aim for roughly one-quarter of the arena in diameter.
  5. Release the mouse. A faint red glow appears in the arena.

Want to modify it?

Right-click the patch to delete it and try again. Larger patches are easier for a first experiment.

Left-click the patch, while pressing Alt to drag it around.

docs.title: Step 3 — Open the network editor
docs.text:
The network editor is where you draw the circuit that connects sensors to motors.

  1. Click the Brain tab.
  2. Click the Network toggle (next to Code brain). In this mode the robot reads its wiring from a file you edit graphically.
  3. Click + beside Network and give the new network a name — for example Braitenberg.
  4. Click ⬡ Open visualizer. The Network Visualizer window opens.

The canvas shows one node already: motor, the left and right wheel outputs (motor_0, motor_1). Everything your circuit builds feeds into this node.

docs.title: Step 4 — Add a light sensor
docs.text:
The robot will sense the gradient patch through a GradientSensor with two rays: one pointing slightly left (light_0) and one slightly right (light_1).

  1. The chip palette is on the left edge of the visualizer (the Palette button shows / hides it).
  2. Drag the GradientSensor chip onto the canvas, to the left of the motor node.
  3. A dialog opens to configure the sensor. Set:
    • name → light
    • n → 2 (one ray per side — left and right)
    • gradient → A (so it responds to the red patch you placed)
    • scale → 60 (this amplifies the raw [0,1] reading to the [-100, 100] motor range)
  4. Confirm. The light node appears on the canvas with two neuron circles (light_0, light_1).

docs.title: Step 5 — Wire for attraction
docs.text:
Now draw a connection from light to motor, and fill in the weight matrix that produces attraction.

  1. Drag from the light node onto the motor node. A connection arc appears and the weight matrix editor opens immediately.

  2. The editor shows a 2 × 2 grid. Rows are target neurons (motors), columns are source neurons (sensors):

    light_0 (left) light_1 (right) motor_0 (left wheel) 0 1 motor_1 (right wheel) 1 0

  3. Choose Manual mode, enter the values above, and confirm.

The canvas now shows two arcs that cross — light_0 feeds motor_1 and light_1 feeds motor_0. That crossing is the wiring that produces attraction.

  1. Click Save in the visualizer toolbar to save the network file.

docs.title: Step 6 — Run it
docs.text:
Close the visualizer (or leave it open beside the main window), then press ▶ Run in the simulator.

Watch the robot. With the patch placed above it, the right sensor (light_1) detects more signal than the left sensor (light_0). Because light_1 drives the left motor (motor_0), the left wheel goes faster and the robot curves right — toward the source. This is Vehicle 2b, attraction.

docs.title: Step 7 — Flip to avoidance
docs.text:
Stop the simulation and change the connection weights to the same-side pattern.

  1. In the network visualizer, right-click the arc between light and motor and choose Edit weight… (or click Weights in the toolbar to open the global weight matrix panel).

  2. Switch the pattern to One-to-one — or, in Manual mode, change the matrix to:

    light_0 (left) light_1 (right) motor_0 (left wheel) 1 0 motor_1 (right wheel) 0 1

  3. Confirm and click Save.

The arcs no longer cross — light_0 feeds motor_0 and light_1 feeds motor_1.

Press ▶ Run again. The robot now moves away from the patch. When the patch is to the right, light_1 fires, the right motor speeds up, and the robot curves left — away from the source. This is Vehicle 2a, avoidance.

docs.title: Step 8 — Keep it moving
docs.text:
Switch back to attraction (Step 5's crossed matrix) and let the robot actually reach the patch. Watch closely: it drives straight through, the patch slides out of the sensor's forward-facing rays, and light_0/light_1 both drop to 0. Since motor_0 and motor_1 are driven directly by those two numbers, both wheels get a flat-zero command — the robot stops dead, wherever the signal happened to run out. Nothing in this circuit gives it a reason to move once there's nothing left to react to. That's not a bug; it's the defining limit of a purely reactive vehicle like this one.

The world updates live

You don't need to stop the simulation to fix this. World edits — placing a patch, dragging it, resizing it — take effect the instant you make them, even while ▶ Run is active. Watch the robot stall, then drop a new A patch a little ahead of it: it should pick the pull back up immediately, no pause or reload required.

Try it

  1. With the robot stalled on an exhausted patch, go to the World tab and click the A button again.
  2. Drag out a fresh patch somewhere ahead of the robot — close enough that its sensor rays can reach it from where it's currently sitting.
  3. Watch it take off again the moment the patch exists. Repeat a few times, dropping each new patch just ahead of wherever the robot ends up, and you can lead it all the way across the arena without ever touching Run/Stop.
  4. Once you've got the hang of it, place four or five A patches around the arena before pressing Run, spaced so each one's radius slightly overlaps the next one's sensing range. The robot should now wander from patch to patch indefinitely instead of stalling on the first one.
  5. Also, try to move the patch around while the simulator is running (Alt+drag) and see if you can make the robot follow your mouse.

Scattering patches works, but it only ever patches the problem over from the outside — the robot itself still has no will of its own. Braitenberg Vehicle III tackles the same stopping problem from the inside instead: one small addition to the circuit that gives the robot a reason to keep moving even with no patches in the arena at all.

Click the Session tab → Save before moving on, to snapshot both the world layout and the brain wiring you've built here.

docs.text:

  • Watching the Brain While You Drive — open the oscilloscope on this circuit and see the sensor and motor signals live as the robot homes in on a patch.
  • Creating Worlds — all gradient, obstacle, and wall types in detail.
  • Analysing a Logged Run — record a run with the Logger, then plot the trajectory and patches in Python.

docs.title: The Belly Rules the Nose — Neuromodulation
docs.text:
A hungry animal and a full one can have exactly the same eyes, nose and wiring, and still behave very differently when they smell food. The difference is not in where signals go but in how strongly they get through. Internal state turns the volume of the senses up or down.

In this tutorial you will build a vehicle that lives in a round arena with two food patches. It circles the arena, eats at one patch, and then ignores the second patch it meets, because a hormone released by its gut is turning down its sense of smell. By the time it comes round to food again, the hormone has worn off. The robot is hungry again and eats. No wire is added or removed between those two moments. Only the gain of the food sensor changes.

What you will build

Step What happens Set up the arena A round arena with two food patches (gradient A) Build an always-hungry vehicle Constant drive, wall avoidance and food approach, the same wiring as Vehicle III Watch it overeat It stops at every patch it meets Give it a gut An InteroceptiveSensor that fills up while the robot eats and releases insulin Put insulin receptors on the nose The food sensor's gain becomes 1 − insulin Watch it skip a meal Fed at one patch, it passes the next one by and eats again once it is hungry

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
Neuromodulators — hormones, neuropeptides — are not point-to-point wires. They flood a tissue and change the gain of every cell that carries the matching receptor. One slow signal retunes a whole pathway at once.

This happens at the first synapse of the olfactory system in both flies (Root et al., 2011) and mice (Oncul et al., 2026): when satiated, circulating insulin reduces how strongly food odours drive the brain. When hungry, the gain is restored. Sengupta (2013) shows the same principle across C. elegans and Drosophila — feeding state routinely gates smell and taste right at the peripheral sensory neuron.

You will build exactly that: a GradientSensor as the nose, an InteroceptiveSensor as the gut that releases insulin onto the neuromodulator bus, and an insulin receptor on the nose that scales its output down when the gut is full.

docs.title: Step 1 — Set up the arena
docs.text:
1. In the Physics tab, set arena_scale to 4 so the arena is big enough to circle.
  2. In the World tab, place two gradient-A patches (the red A button, then drag from the centre outwards). Put one at around North and the other around West, making sure the patches are far enough from the wall to observe a movement from the robot towards them but close enough to allow the robot to sense them with one of its antenae. These are the two meals.
  3. Leave the robot near the middle, slightly left of centre.

docs.title: Step 2 — Build a wall-following robot
docs.text:
Create a new network in the Brain tab (Network mode, +, call it Feeding) and open the visualizer. You'll add three things the robot already knows from the earlier tutorials.

A reason to move. Drag a ConstantLayer onto the canvas, name it drive, n = 2, value = 50. Wire drive → motor with the identity matrix:

drive_0 drive_1 motor_0 1 0 motor_1 0 1

A way to stay off the walls. Drag a DistanceSensor, name it walls, n = 2, angle_spread_deg = 60, max_range = 1.0, scale = 50. Wire walls → motor:

walls_0 (left) walls_1 (right) motor_0 (left wheel) +1 −1 motor_1 (right wheel) −1 +1

A wall close on the left speeds up the left wheel and slows the right one, so the robot turns right, away from the wall. In a round arena this keeps the robot sliding along the boundary. Try it!

Save.

docs.title: Step 3 — Build an always-hungry vehicle
docs.text:
A nose for food. Drag a GradientSensor, name it food, n = 2, gradient = A, angle_spread_deg = 30, scale = 30. Wire food → motor same-side inhibitory, the Vehicle III approach wiring:

food_0 (left) food_1 (right) motor_0 (left wheel) −1 0 motor_1 (right wheel) 0 −1

More food smell on the right slows the right wheel against the constant drive, so the robot curves toward the food (see Braitenberg Vehicle III).

Save.

Press ▶ Run. The robot circles the arena. Each time it passes near a patch, the food smell pulls it in, and it slows and crawls through the patch. Then it continues along the wall to the next patch and does exactly the same thing. It stops to eat at every patch it meets, every lap, forever.

This vehicle has no internal state. Its response to food depends only on what it smells right now, never on what it has already eaten. A real animal that did this would spend its whole life at the food it last found.

docs.title: Step 4 — Give it a gut that releases insulin
docs.text:
1. Drag an InteroceptiveSensor onto the canvas and name it gut. On the Sensor tab set:
    • gradient → A, so it "tastes" the same food the nose smells
    • scale → 1, max_val → 1, start_val → 0 (starts with an empty stomach)
    • tau_rise → 2.0, so about two seconds of eating at the patch centre fills it
    • tau_decay → 5.0, short enough to watch the belly empty in real time
  2. Switch to the Neuron tab and set:
    • neuromodulator transmitter → insulin
    • transmitter color → #FF0000
  3. Confirm and Save.

Don't draw any connection from gut. A transmitter doesn't need one: every tick, gut publishes its output as the value of insulin on the network's neuromodulator bus, and anything that has an insulin receptor reads it. That's the point of a hormone.

gut samples food at the robot's mouth (the front of the body). The deeper the robot goes into a patch, the faster it eats, so a long stay at the edge of a patch fills it as surely as a quick bite at the centre. See InteroceptiveSensor for the full dynamics.

Nothing in the circuit responds to insulin yet — no receptor exists — but the hormone is already being secreted and cleared exactly as intended.

Note

Add gut to the oscilloscope, switch the robot to manual mode and press ▶ Run. Drag the robot onto a food patch and watch the trace climb; drag it away and watch the belly empty over about 5 seconds. Push it in and out a few times — a second visit while the gut is still elevated starts from a higher baseline. If the trace is too small, increase gut's scale factor in the oscilloscope.

docs.title: Step 5 — Put insulin receptors on the nose
docs.text:
One sensory neuron, three knobs

Think of a sensory neuron as two parts. The sensor part transduces the world into a signal and has its own dynamics. That signal is one input to the sensory neuron, which can also receive other inputs (connections from other layers or sensors) and has dynamics of its own. A neuromodulator receptor on the neuron then adds a third, changeable knob.

Stage 1 — The sensor (Sensor tab). Input: raw reading \(r \in [0,1]\). Output:

\[s = f_s(r + b_s) \cdot k_s\]

The bias is added to the raw reading first, the sensor's activation \(f_s\) is applied, and the scale comes last. With \(b_s = 0\), \(f_s =\) linear, \(k_s = 30\) and \(r = 0.5\): \(s = 0.5 \times 30 = \mathbf{15}\). Fixed for the whole run.

Stage 2 — The neuron (Neuron tab). Its input \(u\) is the sensor's signal plus anything else connected to it:

\[u = s + \sum_k W_k\, x_k \qquad y = f(u + b_n) \cdot k_n\]

Same order as the sensor: bias, then activation, then scale. Here nothing else is connected, so \(u = s\), and with \(b_n = 0\), \(f =\) linear, \(k_n = 1\): \(y = \mathbf{15}\). Because \(b_n\) acts on the already-scaled input, a negative \(b_n\) with a relu sets a threshold. Also fixed.

Stage 3 — Neuromodulator receptor. The receptor computes a gain \(g = 1 + k_r\, m\) from the hormone signal \(m\). At site pre it multiplies the neuron's whole input, before the neuron's bias and activation:

\[y' = f(g \cdot u + b_n) \cdot k_n\]

With \(k_r = -1\), \(m = 0.5\): \(g = 0.5\), so \(y' = f(0.5 \times 15 + 0) \times 1 = \mathbf{7.5}\) instead of \(y = 15\): the same stages, the same fixed knobs, a different gain every tick.

That is the whole idea of this tutorial: Stages 1 and 2 are wired once; Stage 3 lets a slow internal signal retune the gain on the fly.

Before wiring the receptor, raise tau_decay on gut to 30 — the 5 s digestion was useful for watching the trace, but the robot needs to stay full long enough to skip the second patch.

  1. Double-click food and switch to its Neuron tab.

  2. Under Modulator receptors, click Add Receptor and fill the row in:

    Modulator Scale Site Mode insulin −1.0 pre absolute

  3. Confirm and Save. Small red circles now appear in the food neurons signaling they are sensitive to the insulin neuromodulator you created.

Each tick, the receptor scales what arrives at food's neuron by a gain:

\[\text{gain} = 1 + \text{scale} \times \text{insulin} = 1 - \text{insulin}\] insulin (gut) gain What the food smell does 0 (empty) 1.0 full strength, strong approach 0.25 0.75 slightly weaker pull 0.5 0.5 half strength, weak pull 1 (full) 0 nothing, the robot is blind to food

Insulin can only turn the food sense down, from 100 % when empty to 0 % when full. It never increases the signal, and it never flips its sign.

Why pre?

A receptor can act at two sites. Call the sensor reading \(r\) and the neuron's output \(y\).

With pre, the gain multiplies the input before the neuron processes it:

\[y = f\!\left((1 + s \cdot m)\, r\right)\]

With post, the gain multiplies the output after the neuron has done its work:

\[y = (1 + s \cdot m)\, f(r)\]

When the neuron is a simple pass-through (\(f(r) = r\)), the two are identical. But once \(f\) is nonlinear — a relu, a leaky filter, a bias — the results differ. A pre gain shifts the neuron's operating point, changing which inputs cross a threshold. A post gain scales the output uniformly, leaving the neuron's internal dynamics unchanged.

Here, food's neuron stage is pass-through, so pre and post give the same result. Using pre throughout the tutorial is the more principled choice: it gates the signal at the input, before any processing, which is the natural model of a presynaptic receptor. In Challenge 1 you will see the difference matter.

Keep the scale at −1 or weaker

With gut capped at max_val = 1, a scale of −1 takes the gain exactly to zero when full — the nose is shut off but never reversed. A stronger scale (e.g. −2) would push the gain negative: food would start to repel the robot instead of just being ignored.

docs.title: Step 6 — Run it: skipping a meal
docs.text:
Press ▶ Run, and add food_0 / food_1 to the oscilloscope alongside gut. You should see a cycle like this:

  1. Hungry. gut is 0 and the gain is 1. The robot is pulled into the first patch it meets.
  2. Eating. With its mouth in the patch, gut climbs over a couple of seconds (tau_rise = 2), faster the deeper the robot goes. The gain falls with it, the food signal fades, and the pull that held the robot in the patch weakens. The constant drive and the wall avoidance take over again, and the robot drifts out of the patch and back onto its path along the wall.
  3. Full, passing food by. The next patch comes up soon after, because the two patches are close together. gut has barely started to empty, so the gain is still low. The weak food signal is not enough to pull the robot off its path, and it skirts the patch and keeps going.
  4. Hungry again. On the longer stretch of wall that follows, gut decays (tau_decay = 30 s) and the gain climbs back towards 1. The next time the robot meets food, it turns in and eats. The cycle repeats every lap.

Now try the receptor scale at 0 (effectively no receptor), −0.5 and −1:

Receptor scale Gain when full Patch it reaches hungry Patch it reaches just after eating none (0) 1.0 eats eats as well, so the robot stops at every patch −0.5 0.5 eats weaker pull, may still turn in −1 0 eats skipped

Same sensors, same wiring, same world. A single receptor on the nose, fed by a signal from the gut, decides which food the robot eats.

It's all about dynamics!

Note that nothing in the network says "skip this patch". After the robot leaves food, gut decays as gut(t) ≈ gut₀ · e^(−t/30). If it leaves with gut ≈ 0.8, then 10 s later gut ≈ 0.57 and the gain is only about 0.43. 60 s later gut ≈ 0.11 and the gain is back to about 0.89. A patch reached soon after a meal is met with a weak nose, one reached much later with a strong one. Change the patch spacing, the starting position or tau_decay, and a different meal gets skipped, or none, or two. This is computation leveraging neural dynamics.

docs.title: Challenge 1 — Hunger turns the gain up
docs.text:
In the circuit you built, a full gut turns the nose down. The relationship can also run the other way: hunger turns the nose up. Build a robot that, when hungry, turns into a food patch from its edge, and that, when fed, only reacts once it is already well inside one, using a receptor with a positive scale.

Solution — what changes and why

  1. Transform satiation into hunger on gut's Neuron tab: bias = −1, scale = −1, transmitter → ghrelin. The neuron computes −(gut − 1) = 1 − gut, so the signal is 1 when empty and 0 when full. The receptor gain is 1 + scale × signal, so a positive receptor on a fullness signal would boost sensitivity when fed — the transmitter has to be high when the robot is hungry.

  2. Make hunger amplify the smell: replace food's insulin receptor with ghrelin, scale +1, site pre. The gain is 1 + ghrelin: 1 when fed, 2 when starving. It must be pre, so the smell is amplified before the threshold of step 3. With post, hunger would only scale the output after the threshold, and a strong smell would get through whether the robot is hungry or not.

  3. Give the smell a threshold: on food's Sensor tab set scale = 10; on its Neuron tab set bias = −3 and activation = relu. The smell now runs from 0 at the patch edge to about 10 at the centre, and the neuron passes only the part above 3. A fed robot (gain 1) gets a signal only well inside a patch, where the smell is above 3. A starving robot (gain 2) doubles the smell first, so a smell of 1.5 already gets through, and it reacts from near the edge, which is where it decides whether to turn in. Don't make the threshold too strict: at −10 even a starving robot's doubled edge smell stays below it, and the robot ignores food altogether. The bias must be on the Neuron tab: the Sensor tab's bias is added to the raw reading (0 to 1) before the sensor's scale, so it would silence the nose instead of setting a threshold (see Sensor bias vs neuron bias).

  4. Make a stronger smell steer, not stall: rewire food → motor as crossed excitation (food_0 → motor_1, food_1 → motor_0, weight +1), the Vehicle II wiring. With the same-side inhibition from Step 3, a doubled smell pushes both wheels toward zero, and the hungry robot stops dead in the patch. With crossed excitation, smell on the left speeds up the right wheel, so a stronger smell just turns the robot harder toward the food.

  5. Keep the smell sharp and the hormone immediate: leave tau_rise and tau_decay empty on food's and gut's Neuron tabs. A time constant on food's neuron smears the smell over seconds and destroys the left/right difference needed for steering. One on gut's neuron adds a second lag on top of digestion, and because the filter starts at 0, the robot begins each run behaving as if it were full.

To see the effect, at least one patch must sit a little off the robot's path along the wall. A patch the robot drives straight over gets crossed whether it is hungry or not; only a patch it has to turn toward shows the difference.

The first lap may look different: the robot starts starving, and the excitation rushes it through the patch rather than slowing it down, so the gut may only half-fill and it eats at the next patch too. If that happens, shorten gut's sensor tau_rise to 1 so a quick pass fills it.

docs.title: Challenge 2 — A hungry animal takes risks
docs.text:
A hungry animal takes risks a fed one avoids. Make the arena's walls hot and place the food patches right against them, so that to eat, the robot has to brave the heat.

Start from the Challenge 1 robot, where gut broadcasts ghrelin (1 when empty, 0 when full). Make the robot avoid the hot walls when fed, and approach the food patches when hungry.

Making the walls hot

In the World tab, select label B, click Wall in the Gradients row and drag inward from the edge. The drag distance sets how far the heat reaches into the arena.
