docs.title: Analysing a Logged Run
docs.text: The Logger in the Session tab records every tick of the simulation to a .jsonl file in logs/ inside your files folder. This page shows how to load one and plot the robots' trajectories together with the arena patches using plain Python and matplotlib.

docs.title: Log format
docs.text:
Each file is a sequence of JSON lines. The first line is a metadata header; subsequent lines are either agent-registration events or tick rows.

{"_meta": true, "version": 2, "arena_scale": 5.0, "arena_round": false,
 "agents": [{"id": 0, "name": "Agent 1", "color": "#4a7fcb"},
            {"id": 1, "name": "Agent 2", "color": "#cc4444"}]}
{"t": 0, "sel": 0,
 "agents": [{"id": 0, "x": 0.0, "y": 0.0, "theta": 1.57, "mL": 0.0, "mR": 0.0,
             "signals": {"light_L": 0.3, "light_R": 0.1}},
            {"id": 1, "x": 1.0, "y": 0.5, "theta": 0.0, "mL": 0.1, "mR": 0.2,
             "signals": {"light_L": 0.6, "light_R": 0.5}}],
 "patches": [{"x": 2.0, "y": 1.0, "r": 0.5, "label": "food", "intensity": 1.0}],
 "objects": [{"x": -1.0, "y": 0.5, "r": 0.15, "color": "#888888"}]}
...

If an agent joins while recording is already running, a registration row is emitted before the first tick that includes it:

{"_agent": true, "id": 2, "name": "Agent 3", "color": "#44cc88"}
Field Type Meaning _meta.version int Format version (2) _meta.agents list Agents present when recording started t int Tick index sel int Id of the selected agent on this tick agents list Per-agent state for this tick agents[i].id int Stable agent id agents[i].x, y float Position (metres) agents[i].theta float Heading (radians) agents[i].mL, mR float Motor commands agents[i].signals dict Sensor outputs (scalar channels only) patches list Gradient patches — same for every row; read from row 0 objects list Solid objects — same for every row; read from row 0

docs.title: Loading the file
docs.text:
import json
from collections import defaultdict
from pathlib import Path

LOG_FILE = r"C:\Users\you\LBPSimulator\logs\sim_20260101_120000.jsonl"

agent_info = {}   # id → {name, color}
ticks      = []   # list of tick dicts
patches    = []
objects    = []
meta       = {}

with open(LOG_FILE, encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for line in f:
        row = json.loads(line)
        if row.get("_meta"):
            meta   = row
            for a in row.get("agents", []):
                agent_info[a["id"]] = {"name": a["name"], "color": a["color"]}
        elif row.get("_agent"):
            agent_info[row["id"]] = {"name": row["name"], "color": row["color"]}
        else:
            if not ticks:
                patches = row.get("patches", [])
                objects = row.get("objects", [])
            ticks.append(row)

arena_scale = meta.get("arena_scale", 5.0)
arena_round = meta.get("arena_round", False)

# Build per-agent arrays
tracks = defaultdict(lambda: {"x": [], "y": [], "theta": [], "t": []})
for row in ticks:
    for a in row.get("agents", []):
        tracks[a["id"]]["x"].append(a["x"])
        tracks[a["id"]]["y"].append(a["y"])
        tracks[a["id"]]["theta"].append(a["theta"])
        tracks[a["id"]]["t"].append(row["t"])

docs.title: Plotting all trajectories
docs.text:
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.patches as mpatches

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 6))
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.set_xlim(-arena_scale, arena_scale)
ax.set_ylim(-arena_scale, arena_scale)
ax.set_facecolor("#1a1a2e")
fig.patch.set_facecolor("#1a1a2e")
ax.tick_params(colors="white")
for spine in ax.spines.values():
    spine.set_edgecolor("#444")

# Arena border
if arena_round:
    border = plt.Circle((0, 0), arena_scale, color="#555", fill=False, lw=1.5)
    ax.add_patch(border)
else:
    border = plt.Rectangle((-arena_scale, -arena_scale),
                            2 * arena_scale, 2 * arena_scale,
                            color="#555", fill=False, lw=1.5)
    ax.add_patch(border)

# Gradient patches
for p in patches:
    halo = plt.Circle(
        (p["x"], p["y"]), p["r"],
        color="#44cc88", alpha=0.25 * p.get("intensity", 1.0), zorder=1,
    )
    ax.add_patch(halo)
    ax.text(p["x"], p["y"], p.get("label", ""), color="#aaffcc",
            ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7, zorder=2)

# Solid objects
for o in objects:
    circ = plt.Circle(
        (o["x"], o["y"]), o["r"],
        color=o.get("color") or "#888", alpha=0.9, zorder=3,
    )
    ax.add_patch(circ)

# Trajectories — one per agent, using its recorded color
for aid, track in tracks.items():
    info   = agent_info.get(aid, {})
    color  = info.get("color") or "#4fa3e0"
    xs, ys = np.array(track["x"]), np.array(track["y"])
    ax.plot(xs, ys, color=color, lw=0.8, alpha=0.8, zorder=4,
            label=info.get("name", f"Agent {aid}"))
    ax.scatter(xs[0],  ys[0],  color=color, s=40, zorder=5, marker="o")
    ax.scatter(xs[-1], ys[-1], color=color, s=40, zorder=5, marker="x")

ax.legend(facecolor="#222", labelcolor="white", framealpha=0.6)
ax.set_title("Robot trajectories", color="white")
plt.tight_layout()
out_path = Path(LOG_FILE).with_name("trajectories.png")
plt.savefig(out_path, dpi=150)
plt.show()

docs.title: Colouring a trajectory by motor command
docs.text:
Replace the trajectory section above with this snippet to colour each segment by the signed turn rate (mR - mL) for every agent:

from matplotlib.collections import LineCollection
from matplotlib.cm import coolwarm

norm = plt.Normalize(vmin=-1, vmax=1)
last_lc = None

# Build per-agent turn arrays from the tick rows
agent_turns = {}  # id → list of (mR - mL)
for row in ticks:
    for a in row.get("agents", []):
        agent_turns.setdefault(a["id"], []).append(a["mR"] - a["mL"])

for aid, track in tracks.items():
    xs, ys = np.array(track["x"]), np.array(track["y"])
    turn   = np.array(agent_turns.get(aid, []))
    if len(xs) < 2 or len(turn) < 1:
        continue
    segments = np.stack([np.c_[xs[:-1], ys[:-1]],
                         np.c_[xs[1:],  ys[1:]]], axis=1)
    last_lc = LineCollection(segments, cmap=coolwarm, norm=norm, lw=1.2, zorder=4)
    last_lc.set_array(turn[:len(segments)])
    ax.add_collection(last_lc)

if last_lc is not None:
    _ = fig.colorbar(last_lc, ax=ax, label="turn (mR − mL)")

Blue segments are left turns, red segments are right turns, white is straight.

docs.title: Reading signal channels
docs.text:
Each agent's signals dict contains its scalar sensor outputs for that tick. To extract a specific channel over time for one agent, select the agent's id and the channel you want to look at:

AID     = 0
CHANNEL = "light_L"

values = []
for row in ticks:
    for a in row.get("agents", []):
        if a["id"] == AID:
            values.append(a["signals"].get(CHANNEL, 0.0))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(8, 4), sharex=True)
axes[0].plot(values, label=CHANNEL)
axes[0].set_ylabel(CHANNEL)

mL = [a["mL"] for row in ticks for a in row["agents"] if a["id"] == AID]
mR = [a["mR"] for row in ticks for a in row["agents"] if a["id"] == AID]
axes[1].plot(mL, label="mL")
axes[1].plot(mR, label="mR")
axes[1].set_ylabel("motors")
axes[1].set_xlabel("tick")
for ax in axes:
    ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

docs.title: A World with Many Vehicles
docs.text:
The simulator can run any number of robots simultaneously, each with its own brain, its own body, and its own sensor readings — all sharing the same arena. This tutorial introduces the multi-agent architecture: how agents are organised into groups, how to run several agents with the same network, and how to stage two groups with different behaviours in the same world.

The focus is on the architecture, not the brain. You will use two networks that ship with the simulator — D01 - AttractionBrain and D01 - AvoidanceBrain — so there is nothing to build before you start.

What you will do

Step What happens Understand groups One group = one network shared by N agents Scale within a group A single spinbox clones an agent N times Add a second group Two groups, two networks, two behaviours in the same arena Position agents Drag discs in the arena to set starting positions Observe the interaction Attraction and avoidance vehicles in the same world

docs.title: Background — groups and agents
docs.text:
The simulator organises agents into groups. Every agent in a group runs the same network — same layers, same weights — but each has its own physics body, its own sensor readings, and its own motor state. Changing a weight or property in the visualizer changes it for every agent in the selected group simultaneously.

A session can have any number of groups, each running a different network. This lets you stage interactions: one group that seeks light, another that flees it; both in the same arena at the same time.

The Brain tab shows one row per group:

Column Meaning Colour swatch The group's display colour — click to change Name Editable label Brain Which network the group runs N How many agents are in the group

docs.title: Step 1 — Load the attraction network
docs.text:
Launch the simulator. In the Brain tab, switch to Network mode. Set Project to 🔒 Simulator → Demos and select D01 - AttractionBrain. The Brain tab shows one group — Group 1 — with N = 1.

Place a single gradient patch (label A) in the arena (World tab → click A → click in the arena). Press ▶ Run: the robot steers toward the patch using crossed excitatory connections. Press ⏸ Pause.

docs.title: Step 2 — Scale Group 1 to multiple agents
docs.text:
Look at the N spinbox in Group 1's row. Change it from 1 to 3.

Three robot discs appear. Press ▶ Run: all three run the identical network independently — same weights, same layers — but each receives its own sensor readings and produces its own motor commands. Watch them converge on the patch from different angles.

Agents don't share state

Each agent has a completely independent activation state. The group only means they run the same network — it is cloned, not shared.

Press ⏸ Pause. Set N back to 1 before the next step.

docs.title: Step 3 — Add a second group
docs.text:
At the bottom of the agent table, click +. A second row appears — Group 2.

With Group 2 selected, switch its network: in the Project selector choose 🔒 Simulator → Demos, then pick D01 - AvoidanceBrain. This network uses the same light GradientSensor and motor layer as the attraction brain, but wired with same-side excitatory connections — the robot steers away from the patch.

The network visualizer follows the selected group

Click Group 1's row — the visualizer shows the attraction network. Click Group 2 — it shows avoidance. There is only one visualizer window; it always reflects the selected group.

docs.title: Step 4 — Position agents in the arena
docs.text:
With two groups, the default start positions overlap. Press ↺ Reset, then drag each robot disc (Alt+drag) to a different position in the arena. The position you drop it on becomes that agent's permanent reset position, saved with the session.

Place both agents at the same distance from the patch, facing it directly. Starting from identical conditions makes the behavioural difference immediately clear: one will drive toward the patch, the other will veer away — purely because of how their sensors are wired to their motors.

Need to rotate the robots?

You can rotate the robots using Alt+Shift+drag.

docs.title: Step 5 — Run and observe
docs.text:
Press ▶ Run. You now have two agents with opposite light responses coexisting in the same arena:

  • Group 1 steers toward the patch and settles near it.
  • Group 2 steers away and orbits the arena perimeter.

Add a second patch (same label A, different position) while the simulation is running. Both groups respond to both patches simultaneously — the sensors detect the maximum signal from all patches of the same label, so the approach agent tracks whichever patch it is closest to, and the avoidance agent keeps its distance from both.

docs.title: Step 6 — Try varying N
docs.text: Select Group 2 and set N to 4. Four avoidance agents appear. Each is repelled from the patch, but their sensor readings differ by position, so they naturally spread around the arena rather than clustering. This emergent dispersion is invisible when you run only one agent.

docs.title: Watching the Brain While You Drive
docs.text: The oscilloscope is a scrolling time-series plot that shows the live state of any node in your network. This page walks through it using the D01 attraction circuit: first with manual drive, then letting the brain take over, so you can see the difference.

docs.title: Step 1 — Set up
docs.text:
1. Open the simulator.
  2. Click the Brain tab, select Network, and load 🔒 Simulator → Demos / D01 - AttractionBrain.
  3. Click the World tab, press the A button, and drag out a gradient patch somewhere in the arena.
  4. Tick ⌨ Manual in the Options row.
  5. Press ▶ Run.

The robot sits still — you are in the driving seat.

docs.title: Step 2 — Open the oscilloscope and watch the motors
docs.text:
Click Osc in the Visualization row. A scrolling plot appears docked at the bottom, already showing the motor channels (motor_0 left wheel, motor_1 right wheel) — the motor node is pinned by default.

Drive the robot around with W / S / A / D and watch the motor traces respond. Check the Real Time checkbox in the top panel if your robot is driving too fast.

Signal too small to see?

Each channel has a multiplier spinner next to its label. Increase it to scale the trace up or down. This allows you to vizualize neurons with different activity ranges.

docs.title: Step 3 — Pin the sensor channels
docs.text:
The motor traces show what the wheels are doing, but not why. Add the sensor to see the full picture.

  1. Open the Network Visualizer (Brain tab → ⬡ Open visualizer).
  2. Right-click the light node.
  3. Choose Add to oscilloscope.

Two new channels appear — light_0 (left ray) and light_1 (right ray). Now drive the robot toward and away from the gradient patch:

Approach head-on. Both channels rise together as the robot closes in; if you come in straight they stay roughly equal.

Approach from one side. The ray pointing toward the patch rises; the other stays low.

Spin in place next to the patch. One ray sweeps through and spikes, then the other — you can read off exactly where each ray is pointing by watching the signal.

Drive through the centre. Both channels peak and drop as the patch slides out behind the robot.

The brain is still running

Manual drive replaces only the final motor command — where the wheel values come from. Everything else keeps running: the sensor rays cast, the weights multiply, the motor layer computes its output. The oscilloscope reflects this: light_0 and light_1 are live sensor readings, and the motor traces show what the brain would have commanded even though you are overriding it.

docs.title: Step 4 — Hand back control
docs.text:
Untick ⌨ Manual (the robot is still running). The brain now drives the wheels.

Watch the oscilloscope: the sensor channels and motor channels are now coupled — when light_1 rises, motor_0 follows (the crossed wiring of the attraction circuit). You can see the full sensorimotor loop unfolding in the plot as the robot homes in on the patch.

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
The same technique works for any node in the network. Right-click any sensor, layer, or motor node in the visualizer and choose Add to oscilloscope to track it. This is useful for:

  • Checking that an intermediate layer is responding as expected before the full circuit is wired.
  • Comparing sensor and motor signals side by side to verify the weight signs are correct.
  • Watching learning layers change their output over time.

docs.title: Braitenberg Vehicle III: Intrinsic Drive
docs.text:
This tutorial picks up exactly where Braitenberg Vehicle II left off. There, the robot only ever moved because something was pulling on its sensors — crossed or same-side, excitatory wiring only ever reacts. You saw the cost of that in Step 8: the instant the patch falls out of sensor range, both motors get a flat-zero command and the robot stops dead, no matter how many patches you scatter to catch it in time.

This time you fix that from the inside: a tiny addition to the circuit gives the robot a reason to move that has nothing to do with what it senses. Braitenberg called this an intrinsic drive, and vehicles that have one — his Vehicle 3 — behave noticeably more like creatures than reflex machines.

What you will build

Step What happens Add a constant drive Both motors get a steady baseline speed from a ConstantLayer — no sensors wired in at all Make the sensor inhibitory The light sensor now subtracts from that baseline instead of adding to it Observe "love" The robot cruises on its own, slows as it nears the patch, and settles close to it instead of colliding or stopping Cross it Same inhibitory wiring, crossed instead of same-side — the robot flees the patch, but, unlike Vehicle II, never stops moving

docs.title: Background — the missing ingredient
docs.text:
Vehicle 3 keeps the exact same body and the exact same sensor as Vehicle 2. Only two things change:

  • The sensor connection becomes inhibitory (a negative weight) instead of excitatory.
  • A ConstantLayer feeds both motors a steady baseline value, completely independent of any sensor.

That baseline is the intrinsic drive: with it, the robot moves even when there is nothing around to react to. The sensor no longer causes motion — it only modulates motion that is already happening, speeding up one wheel relative to the other or slowing the robot down as it nears a source. Braitenberg called the resulting behaviour love: the vehicle approaches a stimulus and settles near it, rather than lunging at it (pure excitation) or needing it just to move at all (Vehicle II's problem).

docs.title: Step 1 — Reopen your Vehicle II network
docs.text:
Launch the simulator, click the Brain tab, and select the network you saved at the end of Vehicle II (named Braitenberg, unless you called it something else). Click ⬡ Open visualizer.

You should see the same two nodes as before: light (a GradientSensor, n=2, scale=60, gradient=A) and motor, however you last wired them. The exact weight matrix on that connection doesn't matter — you're about to replace it.

Skipped Vehicle II?

Build the same starting point: a GradientSensor named light (n=2, gradient='A', scale=60) and a MotorLayer named motor, with one connection between them. See Vehicle II, Step 4 and Step 5, for the details.

docs.title: Step 2 — Add the constant drive
docs.text:
1. Drag a ConstantLayer chip from the palette onto the canvas.
  2. In the dialog, set:
    • name → drive
    • n → 2
    • value → 60
  3. Confirm. The drive node appears with two neuron circles.

ConstantLayer has no separate scale factor — value is the number that reaches the motor. Setting it to 60 matches light's own scale, which will matter once the sensor is wired in (Step 5).

Want to re-organise the layers in your network?

As your network grows, the default placement can get crowded. You can arrange nodes freely in the visualizer: Alt+drag any node to move it to a new position. Use this to place layers side by side horizontally, or stack them vertically to reflect the signal flow — inputs on the left, motors on the right, intermediate layers in between. The image below shows one tidy arrangement for the Vehicle III circuit, with light on the left and the drive and motor neurons aligned in a column on the right.

Note that when two layers share a container (like the motor and drive layers above), the visualizer automatically distributes the nodes so the overall network architecture is symmetrical (like the brain) along the horizontal axis.

docs.title: Step 3 — Wire the drive baseline
docs.text:
Drag from drive onto motor. In the weight-matrix editor, choose Manual and enter the identity matrix:

drive_0 (left) drive_1 (right) motor_0 (left wheel) 1 0 motor_1 (right wheel) 0 1

Confirm and Save.

docs.title: Step 4 — Run it with no patch at all
docs.text:
Go to the World tab and delete every patch in the arena (right-click each one). Press ▶ Run.

The robot drives forward on its own, at a steady speed, with absolutely nothing in the world to react to. Nothing you built in Vehicle II could ever do this — without a stimulus, those motors always read zero. This one keeps going because drive doesn't look at the sensors at all.

docs.title: Step 5 — Make the sensor inhibitory
docs.text:
Stop the simulation. Place an A patch back in the arena (World tab, as in Vehicle II Step 2). Then rewire light's connection into motor:

  1. Right-click the light → motor connection → Edit weight….

  2. Choose Manual and enter the same-side, negative matrix:

    light_0 (left) light_1 (right) motor_0 (left wheel) −1 0 motor_1 (right wheel) 0 −1

  3. Confirm and Save.

Each motor now receives drive's baseline of 60 minus its own-side sensor reading. Because light's scale (60) matches drive's value (60), a sensor reading at full strength cancels its own motor exactly: 60 − 60 = 0.

docs.title: Step 6 — Run it: observe "love"
docs.text:
Press ▶ Run. Far from the patch, both motors sit near the 60 baseline and the robot cruises in a straight line. As it drifts close enough for, say, the left sensor to pick up more signal than the right, the left motor is inhibited more than the right — the relatively faster right wheel turns the robot toward the patch, and it slows the closer it gets. Watch it settle near the patch instead of stopping dead or driving straight through it.

Not settling?

If the robot overshoots and keeps oscillating around the patch, your light scale and drive value may not match closely enough — revisit Step 2 and Step 5's matching 60s, or see the experiment below.

docs.title: Step 7 — Cross it: flee without stopping
docs.text:
Stop the simulation and switch the light → motor matrix to the crossed pattern instead:

light_0 (left) light_1 (right) motor_0 (left wheel) 0 −1 motor_1 (right wheel) −1 0

Confirm, Save, and press ▶ Run again. The robot now steers away from the patch — but unlike Vehicle II's avoidance vehicle, it never goes fully silent. Let it drive straight past the patch and out of sensor range entirely, the same way you did in Vehicle II's Step 8: this time both motors settle back to the 60 drive baseline instead of dropping to zero, and the robot just keeps going.

docs.title: Step 8 — Experiment
docs.text:
Rebalance drive and light

Try drive's value at 100 with light's scale left at 60: the sensor can never fully cancel the baseline, so the robot barely slows down near the patch — the drive dominates. Now try the opposite, light scale 100 against drive value 60: at close range the sensor term overshoots past zero into negative motor output, so the near wheel briefly reverses — a much sharper turn than simple cancellation gives you.

docs.title: Challenges
docs.text:
• Wall avoidance — Vehicle III never stops, which means it will eventually hit a wall. Add a DistanceSensor and wire it so the robot steers away from walls without losing its drive to roam. Think about which vehicle type produces a gentle curve rather than a spin — and whether the wall signal should speed a wheel up or slow it down.

  • Colour vision — Replace the GradientSensor with an RGBCameraSensor and a Conv2dLayer colour filter. The robot can now distinguish objects by colour — approaching green ones and avoiding red ones — using exactly the same crossed and same-side wiring logic you built here. See Braitenberg Vehicles with Vision for a step-by-step guide.

  • Fly courtship — Two groups, two gradient labels, one arena. Place a mounted gradient (label B) on the female's body so the male tracks her position rather than a static patch. For a more realistic version, replace the gradient sensor with a camera and colour filter — the male then responds to the female's actual body colour rather than an invisible cloud. Check out the A World with Many Vehicles page if you don't know how to set up a multi-agent world.

  • On the real robot — Does the same network behave the same way on physical hardware? Wire the Vehicle III circuit to a real robot and see whether the drive baseline and sensor weights you tuned in simulation transfer without adjustment. See Vehicle III on the Real Robot to get started.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Braitenberg Vehicles with Vision — swap the gradient sensor for a camera and teach the robot to tell colours apart.
  • A World with Many Vehicles — put several vehicles in the same arena and watch population-level patterns emerge without changing any brain.
  • Vehicle III on the Real Robot (if you have a robot) — connect the same network to live hardware with no code changes.

docs.title: Vector-Based Homing: Path Integration and Steering
docs.text:
This tutorial builds the compass half of an insect-style path integration circuit — the mechanism desert ants and bees use to walk home in a straight line after a long, winding foraging trip, without retracing their steps. You'll build it piece by piece in the network editor, using the exact parameters shipped in the built-in Demos / D09 - VectorBasedHomingBrain network, and see why each piece has to be there.

The circuit is based on Stone et al. (2017), "An Anatomically Constrained Model for Path Integration in the Bee Brain", simplified down to the compass-only pathway (no optic-flow speed input — this version reads speed from the wheels instead).

What you will build

Part What it does 1. Path integration Combine a compass heading and a wheel-speed signal into a running "home vector" memory 2. Homing Compare that memory against current heading to produce a left/right steering signal

docs.title: Background — why a population code?
docs.text:
A heading can be represented three ways: as (x, y) coordinates, as (distance, angle), or as the amplitude and phase of a single cosine wave. All three are mathematically equivalent — but only the third is biologically realistic, because real neurons can't fire negative, so no single cell can be a signed cosine. Instead, the brain spreads it across a ring of cells, each tuned to a different preferred direction, each individually a clipped (half-wave-rectified) cosine. Added together, population-coded directions still add, subtract, and integrate as if they were cosines — which is exactly what this circuit relies on at every stage.

The ring in this network has 8 cells, each one 45° apart.

docs.title: Step 1 — The compass (TL)
docs.text:
Add a SkyCompassSensor named TL:

Parameter Value n 8 scale 1.0 bias 0.0 phase 0.0 activation relu

Each of the 8 TL neurons outputs relu(cos(heading − sun_dir − k·45°)) — a half-wave-rectified cosine bump, zero for any direction more than 90° from current heading. This is the compass's raw signal: clean, but clipped to flat zero over half the ring.

Ring neurons ≠ ring attractor

Don't confuse this with the biological "ring neurons" (ER neurons) of the ellipsoid body — those are a separate, visual-input cell type. TL here plays the role of E-PG/CL1, the actual compass-bump population.

docs.title: Step 2 — Clean the bump into a true sinusoid (CL1, TB)
docs.text:
Add a RingAttractorLayer named CL1 (n=8, tau_rise=0.1, tau_decay=0.1, activation=relu, bias=0.0). Connect TL → CL1 with the One-to-one preset (Amplitude 1.0, Offset 0) — a straight identity relay.

Give CL1 a self-connection (CL1 → CL1) with an inhibition-dominated kernel: every row's weights must sum to a negative number, with near neighbours inhibited more weakly than far ones, so the ring settles into a single localized bump rather than firing uniformly (see the RingAttractorLayer reference page for the exact bump-formation checklist — row-sum sign, excitatory width, and tonic drive all matter).

Why clean it up at all?

TL's own output is already clipped to zero over half the ring, and a competitive ring attractor's bump is narrow and sharp — neither is a smooth, never-zero sinusoid. The next step needs one.

Now add a LeakyLayer named TB (n=8, tau_rise=0.1, tau_decay=0.1, bias=1.5, activation=relu, scale=0.333333). Connect CL1 → TB with the Cosine preset:

Field Value Amplitude 1.0 Phase₀ 0° Phase step 45° Bias 0

This makes every TB cell a weighted sum of all eight CL1 cells, W[i,j] = cos((i−j)·45°) — a circulant cosine kernel. Mathematically, that's a discrete Fourier filter: it keeps only the ring's fundamental (one-bump-per-revolution) component and discards everything else, reconstructing a smooth sinusoid from whatever shape CL1's bump actually has.

TB's own bias=1.5 and scale=0.333333 then shift that sinusoid so it never touches zero: 1.5 × 0.333333 = 0.5 exactly, so TB oscillates in a band centred on 0.5 (roughly [0.17, 0.83]), always positive. That matters downstream, because the next step multiplies TB by a speed signal — and a signal that still hit zero at some directions would zero out speed in those directions too.

docs.title: Step 3 — Speed, from the wheels (sensor2, TN2)
docs.text:
Add a ProprioceptiveSensor named sensor2 reading the motor joint (use_velocity=false, scale=1.0, bias=0.0, activation=linear) — this is the stand-in for the bee's optic-flow speed signal; a wheeled robot reads wheel rotation instead, which is really closer to a desert ant's leg-based stride integrator than to the original bee's visual odometer.

Add a LeakyLayer named TN2 (n=2, tau_rise=0.1, tau_decay=0.1, bias=0.0, activation=relu). Connect sensor2 → TN2 with a Manual matrix where every entry is 0.005:

\[ W = \begin{pmatrix} 0.005 & 0.005 \\ 0.005 & 0.005 \end{pmatrix} \]

Both TN2 cells end up computing the same number — 0.005·(v_L + v_R), total forward speed — rather than the two differently-tuned channels the real bee circuit uses. That's a deliberate simplification: a wheeled base doesn't have two independent optic-flow axes to split speed across.

docs.title: Step 4 — Gate speed by heading (TBGate)
docs.text:
Add a ProductLayer named TBGate (n=8, tau_rise=0, tau_decay=0, bias=0, activation=linear). A ProductLayer multiplies the totals of its incoming connections instead of summing them — give it two:

  • TB → TBGate: One-to-one preset, Amplitude 1.0 (identity).
  • TN2 → TBGate: Uniform preset, Amplitude 1.0 — every TBGate cell receives TN2_0 + TN2_1 (both channels, summed, broadcast identically to all 8 cells).

So TBGate[k] = TB[k] · (TN2_0+TN2_1) — the instantaneous "am I moving, and which way am I facing" signal for ring position k.

The hidden baseline

Because TB never goes below ≈0.17 (step 2), this product always contains a chunk that has nothing to do with direction: expand TB[k] = 0.5 + wave(k) and TBGate[k] = 0.5·(TN2_0+TN2_1) + wave(k)·(TN2_0+TN2_1). The first term is identical at every ring position — pure contamination from the fact TB can't be silent. Step 5 cancels exactly that term.

docs.title: Step 5 — Integrate into a home vector (CPU4)
docs.text:
Add a LeakyLayer named CPU4 (n=16, tau_rise=0.0, tau_decay=0.0, bias=0.0, activation=hard_sigmoid, scale=1.0, x0=0.5, output_mode=integral).

CPU4 is split into two hemispheres of 8 cells each, both fed by the same TBGate/TN2 signals (since TN2_0=TN2_1 in this simplified version, the hemispheres end up numerically identical here — in the full biological model they'd carry genuinely different ±45°-offset speed channels). Wire two connections:

  • TBGate → CPU4 (Manual, weight -1): each TBGate[k] feeds both CPU4[k] and CPU4[k+8].
  • TN2 → CPU4 (Manual): TN2_0 → CPU4[0..7] and TN2_1 → CPU4[8..15], weight +1 each — this is exactly the term that cancels TBGate's hidden baseline from Step 4.

Both matrices are too big to type out cell by cell, but their shape is simple — each is just two 8×8 blocks stacked, written once with rows 0–7 as hemisphere A and rows 8–15 as hemisphere B:

\[ W_{TBGate \to CPU4} = \begin{pmatrix} -I_8 \\ -I_8 \end{pmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{16\times8} \qquad\qquad W_{TN2 \to CPU4} = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{1}_8 & \mathbf{0}_8 \\ \mathbf{0}_8 & \mathbf{1}_8 \end{pmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{16\times2} \]

where \(I_8\) is the 8×8 identity (one -1 per row, on the diagonal within its own 8-column block) and \(\mathbf{1}_8\)/\(\mathbf{0}_8\) are length-8 columns of all-ones/all-zeros. In the weight-matrix editor that's nothing more exotic than the one-to-one diagonals you've already wired in Steps 2–4 — just stamped down twice, once per hemisphere. Here's what each actually looks like in the editor's own Preview panel (rows = CPU4 target, columns = source; red = excitatory, blue = inhibitory):

  • TBGate → CPU4

  • TN2 → CPU4

Each cell now integrates TN2_hemisphere − TBGate[k], starting from x0=0.5, through output_mode=integral — literally x(t) = 0.5 + ∫(TN2 − TBGate)dt, accumulated once per simulation tick as (…)·dt, not as the raw value itself. Work through the algebra and the hidden baseline cancels exactly, leaving CPU4[k] − 0.5 ∝ −∫v·cos(heading−dir_k)dt — the negative of the outbound displacement, i.e. CPU4 points home, not along the path travelled.

Because the accumulator is never clipped internally (only hard_sigmoid clips the output), this memory has a finite range: travel far enough in one direction and the cells aligned with it saturate, flattening the bump. That's not a bug to fix — real ants and bees have a measurably finite path-integration range too.

You've now built the full path integration half. Load the Demos/D09 - VectorBasedHomingBrain network and compare — TL → CL1 → TB, sensor2 → TN2, TBGate, CPU4 are wired exactly as above (the rest of that network goes further than this tutorial does — see the end of this page).

docs.title: Step 6 — Watch it work: drive manually, watch CPU4 fill up
docs.text:
Before moving on to the readout half, check that CPU4 is actually doing what Step 5's algebra claims, by watching it update live instead of taking the math on faith.

  1. In the Network Visualizer, right-click the CPU4 node and choose Add to activation panel. The panel opens automatically with a 16-bar chart — one bar per CPU4 neuron, bars 0–7 for hemisphere A and 8–15 for hemisphere B.
  2. In the main Controls panel, enable ⌨ Manual (Options row) to drive the robot with the keyboard while the brain keeps running. This does not bypass the circuit — CPU4 is still fed by the exact same TBGate/TN2 signals either way; only who's choosing the heading changes.
  3. Press ▶ Run, then drive in a straight line for a few seconds (W/S forward/back, A/D turn, Space stop). Both hemispheres start flat at 0.5 (that's x0). Watch the bars: because TN2_0 = TN2_1 in this simplified circuit, hemisphere A and hemisphere B should move identically — if they don't, something's wired wrong.
  4. Driving in one direction should push the cell(s) aligned with that heading away from 0.5, while cells roughly opposite stay close to it — Step 5's −∫v·cos(heading−dir_k)dt shape, made visible instead of algebraic.
  5. Turn around and drive back the way you came, same distance: those same cells should drift back toward 0.5. CPU4 accumulates displacement, not "time spent facing each direction" — a loop back to your start should leave it close to where it started too.

Pin TB too

Right-click TB → Add to activation panel and compare the two side by side: TB's bump tracks your current heading instantly, while CPU4 only drifts slowly in response — the difference between a compass and a memory.

docs.title: Part 2 — Homing: reading the vector back out
docs.text: CPU4 holds the home vector, but it's in world (compass) coordinates. Steering needs to know how that compares to current heading.

docs.title: Step 7 — Cross-compare hemispheres (P)
docs.text: Add a LeakyLayer named P (n=16, tau_rise=0.1, tau_decay=0.1, bias=0.0, activation=relu). Connect CPU4 → P with One-to-one, Amplitude 1.0 — a plain relay; P is literally just a renamed copy of CPU4 at this point. (Since this circuit's two hemispheres are numerically identical, this relay doesn't yet do anything interesting on its own — it's set up for the next step.)

docs.title: Step 8 — Compare to current heading (CPU1)
docs.text:
Add a LeakyLayer named CPU1 (n=16, tau_rise=0.1, tau_decay=0.1, bias=0.0, activation=relu, noise_std=2.0, noise_tau=1.5). Wire three incoming connections:

  • P → CPU1: One-to-one, Amplitude -1, Offset 8 — W[i,j] = -1 where j = (i+8) mod 16. This crosses each hemisphere to the other hemisphere's matching ring position, negated.
  • CPU4 → CPU1 (Manual): hemisphere A shifts +1 ring step, within its own 8-cell ring (CPU1[i] = CPU4[(i+1) mod 8], so CPU1[7] = CPU4[0] — it wraps, it does not spill into hemisphere B's columns), hemisphere B shifts −1 ring step the same way (CPU1[i+8] = CPU4[8 + ((i-1) mod 8)], so CPU1[8] = CPU4[15]) — opposite directions, same 45° magnitude.
  • TB → CPU1 (Manual, weight -1): the same TB[i] cell feeds both CPU1[i] and CPU1[i+8] — current heading, unshifted, subtracted from both hemispheres. Same shape as TBGate → CPU4 back in Step 5 — two stacked 8×8 negative identity blocks — just TB (8 cells) in place of TBGate here.

P → CPU1 and CPU4 → CPU1 are both full 16×16 matrices, and neither is a simple stacked block — here's the editor's own Preview for each (rows = CPU1 target, columns = source; blue = inhibitory, red = excitatory):

  • P → CPU1

  • CPU4 → CPU1

Put together (for \(i = 0..7\); the first term wraps mod 8 within hemisphere A, so read CPU4[i+1] as CPU4[(i+1) mod 8] — the CPU4[i+8] term from P needs no such wrap, since i+8 never exceeds 15 here):

\[\text{CPU1}[i] = \text{CPU4}[i+1] - \text{CPU4}[i+8] - \text{TB}[i]\]

Why the opposite shifts?

Shifting CPU4 by +45° on one side and −45° on the other gives each hemisphere a different vantage point on the same stored vector — like sampling it from slightly left-of-centre and slightly right-of-centre. Subtracting the same TB from both breaks the left/right symmetry only when current heading doesn't match the stored direction: pointed straight at the goal, the two hemispheres balance; drift off course, and they diverge — exactly the asymmetry a differential-drive steering command needs. With no shift at all, both hemispheres would be identical and there'd be no way to tell left from right.

Why the noise?

A heading-error signal built from subtracting cosines has not one but two zero-crossings: one where you're facing the goal (a stable point — nudge off it and the signal pushes you back), and one where you're facing directly away from it (an unstable point — nudge off it and the correction grows instead of shrinking, but at that point the signal is exactly balanced with no inherent left/right bias). CPU1's unusually large noise_std=2.0 — far bigger than anything else in this network — exists specifically to kick the system off that knife-edge so it reliably commits to turning one way or the other.

docs.title: Step 9 — Read it out (Steering, Fw, motor)
docs.text:
Stone et al.'s own readout is simple: sum each hemisphere's CPU1 activity and subtract. Add a LeakyLayer named Steering (n=2, bias=0.0, activation=relu, scale=40.0). Connect CPU1 → Steering with a Manual matrix that flat-sums each hemisphere separately: Steering[0] sums all 8 cells of hemisphere A (weight 1 on CPU1[0..7], 0 on the rest), Steering[1] sums hemisphere B the same way — the same flat-sum-per-hemisphere pattern the built-in Demos/D09 - VectorBasedHomingBrain network uses at its CPU1 → DNa03 connection.

A flat sum doesn't work with a raw cosine

Summing a full-period cosine over evenly-spaced ring cells is always exactly zero, for any phase — there is nothing a flat sum could ever pick up from a clean, unclipped sinusoid. This only works because CPU1's own relu (Step 7) has already clipped the negative half of the wave away; a half-wave-rectified cosine does not sum to zero. If you ever build a readout from a layer that hasn't been rectified, project onto a cosine template instead of summing flat, or you'll get zero regardless of the input.

Add a second LeakyLayer named Fw (n=2, bias=40.0, activation=relu) with no incoming connections at all — a constant forward-thrust term, completely independent of the vector circuit. Finally, add the MotorLayer and wire both Steering → motor and Fw → motor with One-to-one, Amplitude 1.0, so motor[i] = Steering[i] + Fw[i].

Gain matters more than you'd think

It's tempting to skip Steering's scale=40 and feed CPU1's hemisphere sums straight into Fw alongside its bias=40. Don't — a raw hemisphere sum, after relu, is typically well under 1; next to a bias of 40 that's a difference of a fraction of a percent between the two motor outputs. The robot will look like it's just driving straight, even though the steering signal is technically present and correctly signed — it's just about 50× too small to matter. Steering's scale is what makes the vector's influence big enough to show up; tune it by watching how sharply the robot corrects course, not by formula. The built-in Demos/D09 - VectorBasedHomingBrain network hides this exact amplification inside DNa02's own scale=50, several layers downstream of CPU1 — easy to lose track of if you're simplifying that circuit by hand.

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
The built-in Demos/D09 - VectorBasedHomingBrain network implements a fuller version of this pathway — Pontine/CPU1 feed into additional PFL2, DNa03, DNa02 layers before reaching motor, rather than the direct Steering/Fw readout built above. Those extra stages come from later Drosophila connectome studies (Namiki et al. 2018; Rayshubskiy et al. 2020; Mussells Pires et al. 2024) layered on top of Stone et al.'s original 2017 bee model, not from Stone's paper itself — Stone's own circuit really does stop at CPU1 → motor (via one amplifying layer and a forward-drive bias), exactly as built above. Worth comparing both once you've built this version by hand.

An interactive explorer for the CPU1 steering computation — sliders for the home-vector and heading cosine waves, live-updating output — lives in this repo's analysis/vector_navigation/ folder (cpu1_steering_interactive.py) if you want to build intuition for Part 2 before wiring it up.

docs.title: Circuits Driving a Real Robot
docs.text:
The simulator can drive a live LBP robot using exactly the same network it runs in simulation — no code changes, no rewiring. This tutorial shows you how: in the Robot tab you tell each sensor and the motor layer where to find their data on the network, switch to robot mode, and the brain runs on hardware.

You will use the D01 - AttractionBrain network that ships with the simulator. It has a light GradientSensor and a motor layer wired for light-seeking — simple enough to verify easily on a real robot, and a good template for wiring any network to hardware.

What you will do

Step What happens Enable robot mode Switch the simulator to live hardware Set the motor address Tell the simulator where to send wheel commands (Robot tab) Verify the connection Confirm the link with manual drive Set the sensor address Map the robot's IR readings to the light node (Robot tab) Test the connection Check everything between the computer and the robot in one go Run the brain live Light-seeking behaviour on real hardware

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Make sure you have the following ready:

  • The name of the Wi-Fi network your robot uses.
  • Your computer connected to that exact same network.
  • The robot's IP address.

The robot communicates over OSC/UDP on port 2390. The simulator sends and receives on that same port — no extra software is needed.

docs.title: Step 1 — Load the attraction brain
docs.text: In the Brain tab, switch to Network mode, set the project to 🔒 Simulator → Demos, and select D01 - AttractionBrain.

docs.title: Step 2 — Enable robot mode
docs.text:
In the left panel, press 🤖 Robot in the Simulation group. The status bar will indicate that robot mode is active.

In robot mode the simulated body is replaced by the real robot: sensor values arrive as OSC packets from the hardware, and each motor command is sent back over the network. The arena view goes dark — there is no simulated world to draw — and the oscilloscope and network visualizer continue working as normal, now reflecting live hardware data.

docs.title: Step 3 — Open the network visualizer
docs.text: In the Brain tab, click ⬡ Open visualizer. You should see the attraction network: a light GradientSensor and a motor layer connected with crossed excitatory weights.

docs.title: Step 4 — Set the motor address
docs.text:
Open the Robot tab in the side panel. It lists every sensor (S) and motor layer (M) of the network, each with its robot address underneath — empty means not connected. In the field under motor, enter:

192.168.0.224:2390/wheels

Replace 192.168.0.224 with your robot's actual IP, then press Enter. The address is saved with the network, and the edit can be undone in the network visualizer like any other change.

The simulator will send /wheels int vleft int vright to this address each step, clamped to [−100, 100].

From the network visualizer

Double-clicking the motor node still shows its robot address, read-only. Edit in Robot tab… next to it takes you straight to the right field.

docs.title: Step 5 — Verify the connection with manual drive
docs.text:
With the motor address set, confirm that commands are actually reaching the robot before going further.

  1. In the Simulation group, press ⌨ Manual to enable manual mode.
  2. Press ▶ Run.
  3. Drive the robot with the keyboard — W forward, S backward, A/D to turn, Space to stop.

What manual mode does

Manual mode does not bypass the brain — the network keeps running every step. It only changes which wheel command gets sent: yours instead of the brain's output. This is exactly what makes it useful here: the brain is live, the visualizer updates, and you can confirm the OSC link is healthy before committing to full autonomous mode.

If the robot responds to your keys, the connection is working. Press ⌨ Manual again to turn it off, then ⏸ Pause before the next step.

While ⌨ Manual is on, the drive keys never type into the Robot tab's address fields, so you can't change an address by accident while driving.

docs.title: Step 6 — Set the sensor address
docs.text:
The robot's light sensors are read from its analog input ports and sent as OSC on /analogs. Each /analogs packet carries five integers: a packet counter followed by four ADC readings (A1, A2, A5, A6). The light sensors should be connected to A1 (left) and A6 (right), which are indices 1 and 4 in the packet.

In the Robot tab, enter in the field under light and press Enter:

192.168.0.224:2390/analogs[iiiii](1,4){x/1023}
Part Meaning 192.168.0.224:2390 Robot IP and port /analogs The OSC address the robot sends sensor readings on [iiiii] Five integer arguments expected (1,4) Extract indices 1 and 4 (the two IR sensors) {x/1023} Normalise raw ADC range 0–1023 to [0, 1]

Use the same IP as the motor address — the sensor data comes back from the robot the motor commands go to.

Scaling

{x/1023} normalises the raw ADC value to [0, 1]. The sensor's own scale parameter then multiplies that result — so the effective range the brain sees is [0, scale]. Set scale on the light node to match the motor range you need, exactly as you would in simulation.

docs.title: Step 7 — Test the connection
docs.text:
Press 🔍 Test connection at the top of the Robot tab. A window works through a checklist and marks each item ✔ passed, ⚠ warning, ✖ failed:

  • the addresses are set up correctly,
  • the robot's port is free on this computer,
  • the robot answers ping (a ⚠ means slow or lost replies — motor commands will lag),
  • the robot sends data back,
  • the light sensor receives /analogs, with its rate and latest values.

Anything that fails comes with the fix — for example the command that lets incoming robot data through Windows Firewall. During the test the robot receives a stop command; robot mode is paused and restored when you close the window. See Testing the connection for what each check means.

docs.title: Step 8 — Run the brain on the robot
docs.text:
Press ▶ Run. The simulator begins sending motor commands and receiving sensor data at approximately 60 Hz. The Robot tab shows each address's live update rate — a red 0 Hz under light means its data isn't arriving.

Point the robot toward a light source that your IR sensors can detect (a bright lamp or a projector patch works well in lab settings). With the crossed excitatory wiring, the sensor on the side closer to the source drives the opposite wheel harder — the robot steers toward the light.

Watch the network visualizer while the robot moves: the light node's neuron activations update in real time from the hardware, and the motor output reflects what is actually being sent to the wheels.

docs.title: Step 9 — Tune for the real world
docs.text:
Simulation and hardware rarely behave identically. Here are the most common adjustments:

Sensor scale doesn't match

Your IR sensors may saturate at a different distance than the simulator's gradient patch did. If the robot steers too weakly toward the source, increase light's scale. If it overshoots and oscillates past the source, reduce it.

One wheel is faster than the other

Real motors have small asymmetries. If the robot drifts left or right when both sensors read equal values, adjust the two connection weights slightly — raise the weight on the path feeding the slower wheel.

Response is too jerky

The motor command changes every step based on the current sensor reading, with no smoothing. Add a LeakyLayer between light and motor (see Wiring Brains) to introduce a time constant — the sensor's influence ramps up and decays gradually, giving the robot a more fluid response.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:

docs.title: Braitenberg Vehicles with Vision
docs.text:
The gradient-patch sensor used in earlier tutorials is a useful fiction: it gives the robot a tidy, single-number reading that represents "how much stimulus is nearby." Real eyes don't work that way. They send the brain a full image, and the brain has to extract from that image the signal it cares about.

This tutorial replaces the gradient sensor with a simulated RGB camera and a small convolutional layer that acts as a colour filter. The resulting Braitenberg circuit can distinguish objects by colour — approaching green ones and avoiding red ones — using the same crossed-and-same-side wiring logic you already know. No code is required.

What you will build

Step What happens Place coloured objects The arena has red and green solid objects Add an RGB camera A lateralized camera gives the robot left and right eyes Add colour-opponent filters A Conv2dLayer extracts redness and greenness from each eye Add a constant drive The robot keeps moving when nothing coloured is visible Wire the motors Crossed weights produce attraction to green, avoidance of red Deploy on the robot Wire the camera to a live ESP32-CAM stream

docs.title: Background — from gradient patches to camera pixels
docs.text:
A GradientSensor ray returns a single float: the stimulus strength at the tip of the ray. That was enough for a colourless world.

A camera returns a 3 × H × W tensor — three colour channels (R, G, B) over a grid of pixels. That's far more information, but the motor layer still expects just two numbers (left wheel, right wheel). Something has to collapse the image down into the numbers the motors need.

This circuit does it in two steps:

  1. Split the image left/right. A lateralized camera gives the left hemisphere the left half of the image and the right hemisphere the right half. The robot now has a "left eye" and a "right eye," just like in the gradient-sensor case.

  2. Apply colour-opponent filters. A Conv2dLayer with a 1×1 kernel treats every pixel independently. Each filter is simply a set of channel weights — [+1, −1, 0] for redness, [−1, +1, 0] for greenness. After global average pooling, each filter returns a single number per eye: how much red (or green) dominates in that half of the view. These two numbers per eye replace what the gradient-sensor ray used to give you.

  3. Wire the motors. The four conv outputs (2 filters × 2 eyes) feed the two motor neurons through a crossed weight matrix. The result is a robot that steers toward green objects and away from red ones.

docs.title: Step 1 — Set up the world
docs.text:
1. Launch the simulator. Click the World tab.
  2. In the Objects row, click + Add object three or four times to place solid coloured circles in the arena. Use the colour picker on each to make two or three of them red and one green.
  3. Drag the objects to spread them around the right half of the arena. Put the green one somewhere in the middle.

Objects are physical — the robot will bounce off them — which is what you want here. The robot's camera will see them as coloured regions as it approaches.

docs.title: Step 2 — Create a new network
docs.text:
1. Click the Brain tab and select Network mode.
  2. Click + beside Network and name the new network VisionBrain.
  3. Click ⬡ Open visualizer. The canvas shows only the motor node.

docs.title: Step 3 — Add the RGB camera
docs.text:
The robot will see the world through a lateralized RGB camera: one image for the left half of its field of view, one for the right.

  1. Drag an RGBCameraSensor chip from the palette onto the canvas, to the left of the motor node.
  2. In the dialog, set:
    • name → camera
    • width → 64
    • height → 48
    • FOV → 90
    • lateralized → ✓ (tick the checkbox)
    • overlap → 0
  3. Confirm. Two image nodes appear: camera_L and camera_R.

With lateralized ticked, the 64-pixel-wide image is split cleanly down the middle: the left 32 columns become camera_L, the right 32 columns become camera_R. Because overlap = 0 there is no shared region — each eye sees a strictly separate half of the scene.

Run it now

Tick ⌨ Manual in the Controls panel, then press ▶ Run. Drive the robot toward the coloured objects with W / S / A / D and watch the two image nodes in the visualizer update as you steer — coloured objects slide in and out of the left and right eyes as the robot turns. Press ■ Stop and untick ⌨ Manual before continuing.

docs.title: Step 4 — Add colour-opponent filters
docs.text:
A Conv2dLayer with a 1×1 kernel acts as a pixel-independent colour filter: it multiplies each pixel by a set of channel weights and then averages the result across the whole image. With two filters you can compute both redness and greenness from each eye simultaneously.

  1. Drag a Conv2dLayer chip from the palette onto the canvas, between the camera and the motor node.
  2. In the dialog, set:
    • name → color
    • n_filters → 2
    • kernel_size → 1
    • pool → global_avg
    • activation → relu
    • scale → 50
    • lateralized → ✓
  3. Confirm. Two neuron-pair nodes appear: color_L and color_R, each with two circles.

docs.title: Step 5 — Connect camera to filters
docs.text:
Drag from camera_L onto color_L. Instead of the usual weight matrix, the Filter Stack dialog opens. It has three parts:

  • Presets (left) — a column of buttons. Each click adds one filter to the stack.
  • Filter stack (middle) — the filters this connection will apply, in order. Each filter becomes one output neuron of color_L.
  • Preview (right) — a heatmap of the selected filter's kernel.

Build the stack:

  1. Click R−G. A filter named R−G appears in the stack. Its kernel weights the red channel +1 and the green channel −1.
  2. Click G−R. A second filter appears below it, with the weights reversed: green +1, red −1.
  3. Click OK.

The order matters: R−G becomes color_L_0 and G−R becomes color_L_1. If you added them the other way round, drag them in the list to reorder, or select one and click Remove selected to start over.

You don't need to wire the right side. Because both the camera and the conv layer are lateralized, the simulator wires camera_R → color_R automatically, with its own copy of the same two filters. Both arcs appear on the canvas.

After relu, R−G is nonzero only when red is stronger than green in that half of the image, and G−R only when green is stronger than red. Each eye now outputs two numbers: how much red dominates on that side, and how much green dominates.

Why 1×1 kernels?

A 1×1 kernel looks at one pixel at a time, so position in the image doesn't matter. Global average pooling then averages over the whole half-image. The robot steers by how much red or green it sees on each side, not by where the object sits within that side. For a Braitenberg vehicle that is enough: more red on the left than on the right means steer left.

Writing your own filter

The presets cover the common colour contrasts. For anything else, click { } Code filter… at the bottom of the Presets column. You write a few lines of Python that assign a NumPy array of shape (in_ch, kH, kW) to W. Here that is (3, 1, 1): three colour channels, one-pixel kernel. The names np, in_ch, kH, kW and the kernel centre ch, cw are predefined.

This reproduces the R−G preset:

W = np.zeros((in_ch, kH, kW))
W[0, ch, cw] =  1.0   # red
W[1, ch, cw] = -1.0   # green

Change the channel weights to build other detectors. For example, W[0] = 1; W[1] = -0.5; W[2] = -0.5 responds to red against both green and blue. Give the filter a name and click OK to add it to the stack.

docs.title: Step 6 — Add a constant drive
docs.text:
Without a baseline, the motors only receive input when a coloured object is in view — the robot stops wherever the colour signal runs out. A ConstantLayer fixes this exactly as it did in Vehicle III.

  1. Drag a ConstantLayer chip from the palette onto the canvas.
  2. In the dialog, set:
    • name → drive
    • n → 2
    • value → 50
  3. Confirm.

The value of 50 is on the same scale as the colour signals: the conv layer's scale of 50 means a half-image full of pure red drives its filter to 50. In practice an object fills only part of the view, so the colour signals stay below the drive and steer the robot without overwhelming it. Raise drive and the robot cruises faster; raise scale and it turns more sharply.

docs.title: Step 7 — Wire the motors
docs.text: Now connect the drive and the four colour neurons to the motor layer, with weights that produce attraction to green and avoidance of red.

docs.title: Drive → motor
docs.text:
Drag from drive onto motor. In the weight-matrix editor, choose One-to-one (or enter the identity matrix manually):

drive_0 drive_1 motor_0 (left) 1 0 motor_1 (right) 0 1

Confirm.

docs.title: color → motor
docs.text:
Drag from color_L onto motor. You only make this one connection. Because color_L and color_R are a lateralized pair, the weight-matrix editor covers both eyes at once: 2 rows (the motors) and 4 columns (the four colour neurons).

The columns follow the order the neurons are drawn on the canvas, top to bottom. The right eye is drawn mirrored, so its two neurons come in reverse order:

Column Neuron Meaning 1 color_L_0 red, left eye 2 color_L_1 green, left eye 3 color_R_1 green, right eye 4 color_R_0 red, right eye

Choose Manual and enter:

red L green L green R red R motor_0 (left wheel) 1 0 1 0 motor_1 (right wheel) 0 1 0 1

Confirm. Click Save in the visualizer toolbar.

Read the matrix one colour at a time:

  • Green is crossed. Green on the left drives the right wheel; green on the right drives the left wheel. This is Vehicle II's attraction wiring.
  • Red is same-side. Red on the left drives the left wheel; red on the right drives the right wheel. This is Vehicle II's avoidance wiring.

The matrix is symmetric when you mirror it left-to-right: each eye is wired the same way as the other, just onto the opposite wheel.

docs.title: Step 8 — Run it
docs.text:
Close the visualizer (or leave it open alongside the arena). Press ▶ Run.

Watch the robot. When a green object is on its right, color_R_1 fires and speeds up the left wheel, so the robot turns right, toward the green object. When a red object is on its right, color_R_0 fires and speeds up the right wheel, so the robot turns left, away from the red one.

Away from any coloured object, all four colour neurons sit near zero (relu removes the negative values), so both wheels run at the drive baseline of 50 and the robot drives straight.

Understanding the weight logic

This is the gradient-sensor Braitenberg wiring applied twice, once per colour: crossed for green (attraction), same-side for red (avoidance). Both run at the same time, so when red and green are both in view the two pulls compete, and the stronger colour signal wins.
